title: The Alembic
subtitle: Data Visualization II · multiple mappings + solvent selection
story: You wake to alarm bells and a floor tilting under your boots. There is a cold, spreading mark on your forearm, where some alien sickness slipped under your skin as you came aboard. This is the Alembic, a brass-and-canvas airship adrift over a world of floating islands, and she is listing further by the minute, sliding toward a crash. There are medical test stations around the ship: cure yourself by working your way through them all, down to the engine room that will dispense the one solvent that will cure you by poisoning the sickness, then unlock the bridge to take the wheel and avoid a crash!
enterLabel: Check the mark on your arm →

done.title: The cure!
done.body: You've named it — the one solvent that won't mix with water, sits at middling polarity, and rides lighter than water. You program that answer in and that solvent bubbles up in the funnel on the front of the console. You put it on the wound, and see the lesion begin to heal. Now all that's left to do is open the ship's bridge, and avert a crash.

escapeDone.title: Home by the stars
escapeDone.body: Up in the crow's nest the captain's astrolabe turned under your hands — three views of one sky — and only a single star holds its place in the Anchor through every one of those views. You set the wheel to its bearing. The Alembic answers, banking off the black crags and climbing into clean night!

rooms.designNote: TEACHING ROOM 1 — THE APOTHECARY BAY. Story: the player finds the cold alien lesion on their arm and a brass field TEST-KIT; the ship's medicine and its door-locks both run on the same solvent rack, so curing themselves and reaching the helm are one problem. This station reads the FIRST property of the cure (e.g. it must NOT mix with water — read miscible_with_water). Per the pre/post principle, pose it as a MULTI-VARIABLE MAPPING plot (map several solvent properties to aesthetics, read one off) — NOT a single-column filter — mirroring hospital's question style. Solving narrows the cure AND releases the door onward. ALSO the home of the brass mapping DIAL (obj_dial): flipping it sets gameState.mapping to a sigil (m1/m2/m3); its effect isn't explained or visible here — it drives the crow's-nest chart much later (Riven: a control changing a distant display). Exact MCQ/plot TBD in the teaching-room design pass. || DOOR LOCK (2026-07-31): the hatch DOWN to the cargo hold is now a LOCKED forward door gated on THIS room's puzzle — solving the apothecary reading unlatches it (the up-hatch to the deck stays open).

check.prompt: This medical test station asks about solvents that will NOT dissolve into water — prove how mixing with water relates to a solvent's polarity. Work it out from the data: assign the mean relative_polarity of the water-mixing solvents to mixers, and the mean relative_polarity of the non-mixing solvents to nonmixers.
check.expr: is.numeric(mixers) && is.numeric(nonmixers) && mixers > nonmixers && abs(mixers - 0.5358) < 0.02 && abs(nonmixers - 0.1865) < 0.02
check.hint: Split the rack by miscible_with_water (a TRUE/FALSE column) and take the mean relative_polarity of each group: solvents |> group_by(miscible_with_water) |> summarise(m = mean(relative_polarity)). The TRUE group is your mixers, the FALSE group your nonmixers.

feedback.correct: Correct — noted in your field notebook: the water-mixers are far more polar (mean ~0.54) than the water-shy solvents (mean ~0.19). Your cure won't mix with water, so it lives among the low-polarity, water-shy solvents.
wrong: Group the rack by whether it mixes with water and average the polarity of each group: solvents |> group_by(miscible_with_water) |> summarise(m = mean(relative_polarity)).
Read the two group means off that summary and assign them: the TRUE (mixes) group's mean to mixers, the FALSE group's mean to nonmixers.
The solvents that mix with water are the MORE polar group — your mixers mean should be the larger of the two.

rooms.designNote: TEACHING ROOM 3 — DEEP IN THE HOLD. THE TAUGHT TRAP (reworked 2026-07-22). Story: the test-kit now faces the cure's own family. Room 1 established the pooled rule — water-mixers are the more polar solvents. Here the player facets by category and looks inside the ALCOHOLS, where that rule collapses: 2-propanol mixes with water yet is LESS polar (0.546) than 1-butanol (0.586), which doesn't; polarity can't separate the alcohols, but density (chain length) does, cleanly. Load-bearing — the cure (1-butanol) is itself one of the polar-but-immiscible exceptions. Dark, cavernous hold; the plot lives on the laptop. Mirrors hospital's room-3 facet subversion. Verified vs solvents.csv; correct = idx 2. || DOOR LOCK (2026-07-31): the bulk-door DOWN to the engine room is now a LOCKED forward door gated on THIS room's puzzle — solving the hold reading unseals it.

question.prompt: This medical test stations asks about solvents that mix with water, in other words, the more polar ones. Look inside one family, the alcohol family, coloured by whether they mix with water: what actually separates the alcohols that mix from those that don't?
options: The same rule holds — the alcohols that mix are simply the more polar ones
Nothing separates them — every alcohol mixes with water
Polarity barely separates them; it's the heavier, longer-chain alcohols that stop mixing, so density tells them apart — not polarity
The alcohols that mix are the denser ones
Only chlorinated alcohols fail to mix
The alcohols that don't mix are simply the least polar ones

feedback.correct: Exactly — inside the alcohols the polarities overlap, but density (chain length) decides. Only two polar alcohols refuse to mix with water: 1-butanol and 1-octanol — and your cure is one of them. The sealed bulk-door down to the engine room grinds open.
wrong: Split the rack into small multiples by category and look only at the alcohol panel; colour by miscible_with_water, and check whether polarity actually separates the two colours.
Inside the alcohols the polarities overlap — two that don't mix sit right among ones that do. Compare their densities instead.
The alcohols that refuse to mix are the heavier, longer-chain ones — read density, not polarity.

rooms.title: The crow's nest
rooms.technique: escape — read the dial-driven star-plates (multiple mappings)
rooms.designNote: ESCAPE part 1 — THE CROW'S NEST (deep night, high on the mast, 'see the whole', very Riven). STAR REDESIGN 2026-07-22 (was solvent charts). The captain's star-astrolabe (obj_chart, a mapview) shows a field of NAMED STARS under whichever plate the room-1 astrolabe plate-dial selects (m1/m2/m3) as a pre-rendered PNG. Each plate projects the same stars a different way; the Anchor (homeward house) is marked on every plate. Exactly one star — SOLIRA — holds the Anchor across all three plates; its NAME is the helm lock. The star-log clue (obj_starlog) names the Anchor + the method, not the answer. Fully data-free (no solvents). PNGs + answer from nest/make_starchart.py; equal-length star names keep the lock a fixed length. The plate-dial is co-located here beside the astrolabe (moved out of room1 so there's no cross-ship back-nav during the escape); the player turns it, reads each plate, takes the intersection → SOLIRA → helm.

authoring.scenePrompt: This is a seamless 360-degree panorama from the centre of the crow's nest atop a steampunk airship, a small round railed platform high on the mast. Directly behind the viewer, split across the extreme left and extreme right edges, is an open, unbroken stretch of star-blazing night sky over dark floating islands far below, rigging lines rising to the gas-bag above: the far-left edge and the far-right edge are the two halves of this one surface and must match exactly in colour, texture, and lighting, joining into a single continuous, unbroken whole when the image wraps left to right. To the left of centre, the captain's great brass STAR-ASTROLABE on a swivel mount — a tall ringed instrument with a large engraved circular star-plate showing the current plate of named stars; to the left of centre, a heavy BRASS PLATE-DIAL with three engraved marks and a needle for turning the astrolabe to a new plate; dead ahead in the centre, a railed ratline and ladder leading DOWN the mast to the weather deck below; just right of centre, a chart table holding an open leather star-log naming the homeward house, and a spyglass; to the right, a glowing signal lantern and a windsock snapping at the rail. Cold, constant starlight and warm brass highlights, wind-torn cloud, film grain, richly detailed. No people, no lettering, no captions, no text. Again: the extreme left and right edges must align perfectly into an open, unbroken stretch of star-blazing night sky over dark floating islands far below, rigging lines rising to the gas-bag above, with no visible seam, join, or repetition.

rooms.debrief: No solvents, no console — the boss's move made into stars. The captain's astrolabe showed one sky under three projections, and the star-log named the homeward house without naming the star. Exactly one star — SOLIRA — sat inside that house across all three plates, the same 'in-region under every mapping' reasoning that had picked 1-butanol out of the rack. Its bearing keyed the deck hatch, the wheel appeared, and the Alembic climbed for home.

coverPrompt: Minimalist stylised thumbnail poster of a lone steampunk airship — a brass-and-canvas vessel with a great gas-bag and a tall mast crowned by a small crow's nest — adrift over an archipelago of floating islands at nightfall. One bold, simple, high-contrast silhouette of the ship against a sky that gradients from deep green-violet dusk at the horizon to a star-blazing indigo night above, a single bright bearing-star high in the upper sky. Iconic and uncluttered. Flat, limited palette: brass gold, verdigris teal, deep indigo, dusk violet, one warm lamplit window-glow. Soft film grain, painterly but clean, simple geometric shapes, strong negative space, single centred focal subject. No people, no text, no lettering, no logos. Square composition.

debrief.title: How this world worked
debrief.intro: The whole flight was one skill dressed as a rescue: reading a many-variabled plot the right way — a relationship, a group that crosses a line, a within-group split — to pull one honest answer out of a crowded table. Each medical station drilled a different way of looking; the engine room made you name the single solvent that satisfied every mapping at once; and the escape put the same move in the night sky, hunting the one star that keeps its place through every projection. Here is how each part taught the reading.
